video_title: The Best Bear Case on AI | Animal Spirits 478
gist: Ben Carlson argues the 2020s are shaping into one of the greatest bull markets ever (S&P 500 +15.7%/yr, broadening to equal-weight, small caps, Europe, EM, with tech up 65% since Jan 2025 while its forward P/E fell from 29 to 22), while Michael Batnick pushes back that the real bear case is that earnings are too good to last. On AI they explicitly refuse to take a side, calling Paul Kedrosky's capex/ROI argument the best bear case available and putting the bubble question in the too-hard pile, while noting Anthropic's $65B revenue run rate and $3T of hyperscaler spending that is bigger than reported because of off-balance-sheet leases. Secondary threads: 3% real TIPS yields as an ignored opportunity, money-market 'cash on the sidelines' debunked, the Gen Z sports-betting survey being badly misread, and 32 proposed NHL-franchise ETFs.

themes.theme: Bull market breadth and the earnings-too-good bear case

insights.claim: The 2020s S&P 500 has compounded at 15.7% per year versus 13.4% in the 2010s, putting the decade within reach of the 1980s (~17%) and 1990s (~18%) as one of the greatest bull markets in history.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Frames current returns as late-cycle-great rather than merely good; investors sizing forward return assumptions off the last five years are extrapolating a top-decile decade.

insights.claim: Vanguard's total stock market index (VTI) is up almost 1500% in total, roughly 17% annualized, since the March 2009 bottom, which Ben Carlson dates as the start of the current bull market despite Michael Batnick's objection that a bear-market bottom is not a bull-market start.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Anchors the magnitude of the run for anyone modeling mean reversion; a 1500% cumulative move is the base rate a bear case has to argue against.

insights.claim: The bull market has broadened decisively in the last 24 months: new all-time highs have been hit in the S&P 500, the equal-weight index, Europe, midcaps and small caps, with emerging markets basically there, which kills the 'it's only the Mag 7' caveat that dogged the rally.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Broadening leadership argues for equal-weight, small-cap and international exposure rather than doubling down on mega-cap concentration.

insights.claim: Tech stocks are up 65% since January 2025 while the sector's forward P/E has fallen from 29 to 22, meaning earnings have outrun price - the opposite of a classic multiple-expansion bubble.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: The single strongest anti-bubble data point in the episode: valuation-based shorts on tech are fighting falling multiples, not rising ones.
insights.quote: In that time the forward PE has gone from 29 to 22 while the stocks have risen almost 70%.

insights.claim: The live bear case is no longer that earnings are fake but that they are too good and therefore temporary, a worry that Michael Batnick concedes is legitimate even though it sounds absurd.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Reframes the risk from valuation to the E in P/E: watch margin sustainability, not multiples, as the thing that breaks this market.
insights.quote: But honestly, that is part of the bare case is that the earnings are too good.

insights.claim: Median S&P 500 earnings growth - which strips out the hyperscaler distortion - is running around 14%, the highest in a long time and far above normal, per a Wall Street Journal chart sourced from Bank of America.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Rebuts the claim that index earnings are just an AI markup; but a 14% median is also the peak-growth level that would mean-revert in a slowdown.
insights.quote: strip out the one time like the hyperscalers, the median earnings growth is about 14%

insights.claim: Single-variable explanations of the bull market fail cross-sectionally: Europe had negative rates in the 2010s without a boom, and in the 2020s China borrows as much or more as a share of GDP than the US while MSCI China is up only 2% in total for the decade.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Deficit-spending and QE explanations for US equity returns don't survive an international control group - a reason to discount macro-liquidity-only bear or bull cases.
insights.quote: MSEI China has done literally nothing this decade. It's up 2% in total in the 2020s.

insights.claim: A secular bull market can only be identified in hindsight - nobody was calling the 2010s a bull market in 2010 or 2011, when the debate was still about a double dip, and the first bull-market talk came in 2013.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Cautions against timing entries on regime labels; the same logic implies today's 'greatest bull market' framing is itself only knowable later.
insights.quote: a secular bull market can only be defined in hindsight. It can't be defined in the moment.

insights.claim: Ben Carlson expects no correction and another 20% up year in the stock market, delivered half-jokingly as the episode's closing prediction.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: A tell on how bullish sentiment has become among mainstream commentators - itself a contrarian input worth tracking.
insights.quote: I mean, we're going to have another 20% up year in the stock market, it appears.

themes.theme: AI capex bear case vs. real AI revenue

insights.claim: The AI debate maps onto the old hard-landing/soft-landing fight: technologists have been right about the explosion in capabilities while economists have been right about the muted economic impact, and both camps stay half-right indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson, citing Alex Eis
insights.so_what: Suggests the base case is neither AGI-driven productivity boom nor bust, which argues against binary AI trades and for position sizing that survives a long middle.
insights.quote: technologists have largely been right about the massive increase in capabilities

insights.claim: Paul Kedrosky's AI bear case - made on the Big Technology podcast - is that AI capex is the largest spending as a percentage of GDP in history, it arrived faster than any prior buildout, and the ROI simply will not arrive in time given everything else that must be funded.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick and Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: The cleanest articulation of the bear case for AI infrastructure exposure - the risk is timing of returns, not whether the technology is real.
insights.quote: it's not just that it's the biggest spending as a percentage of GDP in history. It's that it happened faster than any time in history

insights.claim: By his own framing, the AI bear is only wrong if the buildout turns out to be a call option on AGI, which the hosts paraphrase as needing to turn technology into a god for the numbers to work.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson, describing Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Defines the binary explicitly: owning AI infrastructure at these prices is an implicit long AGI-optionality position, which is how it should be sized.
insights.quote: unless we get unless we turn technology into a god

insights.claim: Even the most credible AI bear is not shorting it - asked how he was betting the thesis, Kedrosky said not really, that he could not force himself to put the trade on.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: A well-argued bubble thesis with no expressible trade is a warning about timing risk and borrow cost, not an entry signal.
insights.quote: Not really. I can't really force myself to put it.

insights.claim: Both hosts explicitly put the AI bubble question in the too-hard pile, arguing that no outside investor can know whether Google, Microsoft and Amazon will earn an adequate return on their AI investment.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: An honest epistemic stance from mainstream commentators; it implies staying market-weight rather than expressing a view either way in hyperscalers.
insights.quote: I don't know how could I how could I know how could I know if if if Google and and Microsoft and Amazon are going to get a high enough return on their investment.

insights.claim: The headline $3 trillion of hyperscaler AI spending understates the real commitment because Google, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, Amazon and Nvidia carry massive off-balance-sheet leases that have not started yet, per the Wall Street Journal.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Reported capex understates true obligations - credit analysts and equity holders should model lease commitments before assuming free-cash-flow coverage.
insights.quote: these massive offbalance sheet leases that have not started yet

insights.claim: Hyperscaler AI spending has already passed through free cash flow into borrowing territory, and Google has even issued equity to fund it.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: The funding mix shifting from cash to debt and equity is the mechanism by which an AI capex slowdown would transmit into credit spreads and dilution.

insights.claim: Anthropic's revenue run rate has reached $65 billion, exceeding the trailing twelve-month revenue of Pfizer, Cisco, ConocoPhillips and Intel, running $10 billion ahead of Uber, $15 billion ahead of Coca-Cola and roughly $17-18 billion ahead of Netflix, and about to pass Oracle and Delta.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Hard evidence that AI demand is real revenue and not just circular vendor financing - the strongest counterweight to the capex bear case.
insights.quote: $10 billion ahead of Uber, $15 billion ahead of CocaCola

insights.claim: That Delta still books more revenue than several of these companies is a reminder that revenue scale says nothing about business quality, and mainly shows how poor a business airlines are.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Guards against revenue-comparison charts as a valuation shortcut; margins and capital intensity, not run-rate revenue, determine what a business is worth.

insights.claim: AI memory names came roaring back immediately after their selloff, with SanDisk up 35% in a single week, and the rebound got a fraction of the attention the decline did.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Illustrates how violently AI-adjacent hardware mean-reverts; drawdowns in memory names have been buying opportunities rather than regime changes so far.
insights.quote: San Disc was up 35% last week.

insights.claim: Chip engineers at Samsung and SK Hynix earning mid-six-figure bonuses have become the most sought-after bachelors in South Korea, with one interviewee saying her biggest regret from three years of dating an SK Hynix employee was not buying the stock.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson, citing the Wall Street Journal
insights.so_what: A textbook late-cycle social indicator for the semiconductor boom - the kind of cultural signal that historically appears near the enthusiasm peak of a capex cycle.
insights.quote: I dated a guy who worked at SKHEX and for three years, and my biggest regret is that I didn't buy the stock.

themes.theme: Bonds, cash and the ignored 3% real yield

insights.claim: The $3 trillion of retail money in money market funds that gets cited as cash on the sidelines is only 11% of S&P 500 market cap, below the 18% average since 1990, so the denominator adjustment kills the bullish sidelines narrative.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Removes a widely-cited bull argument; cash is not unusually high relative to equity market cap, so do not underwrite a wall of money flowing into stocks.

insights.claim: Money market fund assets were 61% of stock market capitalization in 2009 - roughly double the dot-com peak level - which was largely a denominator collapse rather than genuine hoarding.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick and Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Historical context showing the cash/market-cap ratio is mostly a market-level indicator in reverse, not a standalone sentiment gauge.
insights.quote: That is bananas that it was that money market funds were 61% of the stock market 2009.

insights.claim: Cash has structurally replaced bonds as the fixed income allocation for many investors, who were scarred by losing roughly 18% in bonds and now prefer a barbell even at lower yields.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Implies persistent structural demand for T-bills and money funds and weaker demand for duration, which matters for term premium and long-end supply absorption.
insights.quote: Cash is my bond allocation and even if I get lower rates and lower yields, I'm going to have a barbell portfolio

insights.claim: William Bernstein argues 20-to-30-year TIPS yielding about 3% real is a massive buying opportunity, given TIPS real yields fell below 2% by 2010, below 1% by 2011, and the 5-year TIPS yield hit negative 1.76% in 2021.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson, citing William Bernstein
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable long-duration real-yield trade for anyone who believes inflation stays near 3%; the historical distribution says 3% real is near the high end.
insights.quote: In 2021, the 5-year tips yield fell to negative 1.76%.

insights.claim: Nobody wants TIPS at 3% real because investors think in nominal terms and their hands still hurt from the 2022 bond drawdown, which is exactly why the opportunity persists.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: A behavioral explanation for why real yields stay attractive; recency-driven aversion to fixed income volatility is the source of the premium.
insights.quote: Their hands still hurts from touching the oven. They don't want volatility in their fixed income.

insights.claim: Strategas strategists, asked on Steve Eisman's podcast what bond yield would pull money out of stocks, said the level is well above the 4-4.5% the hosts assumed - a pure bull-market mindset in which a 5% bond yield is irrelevant against 20% equity returns.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson, citing Jason Trennert / Strategas
insights.so_what: The equity-to-bond switching level is higher than consensus assumes, meaning rising yields alone are unlikely to trigger a rotation until returns break.
insights.quote: if you're getting 20% a year in the stock market, what do you care if you can get four or five or 6% in the bond market?

insights.claim: Michael Batnick's operative threshold on long rates is path-dependent: a lurch in the 30-year yield from 5% to 6% would make the stock market buckle, while a steady march higher would keep being absorbed.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Gives a watchable trigger - speed of the move in the long end, not the level - for when rising yields become an equity problem.
insights.quote: if the 30-year goes from if it lurches from five to six, the stock market will buckle, but if it's a steady march higher, I don't know where the line is

insights.claim: Equities have fully absorbed a regime nobody would have believed four years ago - 6% mortgage rates, 5% bond yields and rising long-end yields globally - with the median stock at an all-time high.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: The rates-equity linkage that most models assume has empirically broken; discount-rate-based bear cases have already been wrong for years.

themes.theme: Retail beating professionals and the limits of market efficiency

insights.claim: The right operating premise is not that the market is always right but that it is hard to know when the market is wrong - Burton Malkiel's version being that prices are always wrong and what is right is that nobody knows whether they are too high or too low.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick, citing Burton Malkiel
insights.so_what: A usable working definition of efficiency for active investors: the bar is not mispricing existing, it is knowing the direction of the mispricing.
insights.quote: the price is never right and in fact prices are always wrong. What's right is that nobody knows for sure whether they're too high or too low.

insights.claim: For 15 years beating the market required only buying the biggest, best-known names - no satellite imagery, alternative data, algorithms or complex models - which is why professional investors have been so thoroughly beaten by ordinary retail holders.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Explains the collapse of the active management edge and warns that the alpha source of the last cycle was simple concentration, which can reverse just as simply.
insights.quote: to beat the market, all you had to do was buy the big names that every Joemo has heard of. No need for any satellite imagery, data, sophisticated algorithms, or complicated Excel models.

insights.claim: Michael Batnick names the only environment where he would outperform the average retail investor: a bear market where buying the dip stops working, because a diversified investor down 30% will not blow up while the person in the 3x leveraged Nasdaq fund will be down 80%.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Identifies the precise regime that would reverse the retail-over-professional scoreboard, and flags leveraged product holders as the point of maximum fragility.
insights.quote: The guy in the leverage the three times leveraged NASDAQ fund is going to be down 80%.

insights.claim: A large cohort of professional investors actively needs the era of the best-known mega-cap companies beating everything to end, which is itself a positioning and sentiment signal.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Widespread professional desire for a regime change is a reason to distrust bearish mega-cap research as motivated rather than analytical.
insights.quote: There's a lot of professional investors who want this era of the best and most well-known companies beating everything. People want need that era to end.

insights.claim: Value, dividend and international stocks are working right now, but a genuine regime change requires tech getting smoked for a sustained period rather than a few quarters of relative strength.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Sets the bar for declaring a style rotation: relative outperformance without tech underperformance is not the regime the value crowd is waiting for.

insights.claim: The market has been a first-level thinking market for a long time, rewarding the obvious trade over sophisticated analysis.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Frames when complexity gets paid; a shift to second-level markets would be the signal that research-intensive strategies start earning their fees again.
insights.quote: It's been the first level thinking market for a long long time.

themes.theme: Gambling products, sports-betting ETFs and misread survey data

insights.claim: The viral Betterment survey stat - 26% of Gen Z investors treating sports betting as a deliberate ongoing part of their financial plan versus 14% of millennials and 6% of Gen X, from an online survey of retail investors - is one Ben Carlson flatly does not believe.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: The headline number driving the financial-nihilism narrative is the input many analysts use to size the sports-betting TAM; treat it as unreliable.

insights.claim: Going to the actual Betterment source undercuts the headline: 36% of Gen Z do not participate in sports betting at all, 15% used it to accelerate a goal, 14% occasionally redirected funds, 23% kept funds separate as fun money, and only 11% treat it as a high-risk investment strategy.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: One in ten, not one in four, is the real degenerate-gambler share - a materially smaller base for both the doom narrative and sportsbook revenue projections.
insights.quote: So 36% of Gen Z people just don't bet. 15% used it to accelerate a goal.

insights.claim: A filing has been submitted to register 32 ETFs tied to each individual NHL franchise, each investing in futures contracts on the CME index for that team - and it is notable that the NHL got there before the NFL or NBA.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson, citing Jeffrey Ptak
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that the ETF wrapper is being extended to pure sports speculation; watch whether exchanges and issuers get regulatory pushback.
insights.quote: filing to register 32 ETFs tied to each NHL franchise. Each ETF will invest in futures contracts tied to the CME FSPI index for the team concerned.

insights.claim: The hosts predict sports-gambling ETFs will fail to gather assets because a high-probability, steady-return product strips out the ecstasy and agony that is the entire point of gambling - and clipping 8% a year is not why people bet.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson and Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: A non-obvious product thesis: gambling demand is entertainment demand, so securitizing it destroys the demand - and if there is edge, it accrues to firms like Jane Street, not retail funds.
insights.quote: yay I'm clipping 8% a year because I'm I'm betting taking all the high favorites or something. Like what is the fun in that?

insights.claim: The asset-gathering success or failure of these sports ETFs will serve as a real-money test of whether the viral Gen Z gambling survey numbers are true.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Gives a falsifiable, observable metric - flows into team ETFs - for a narrative that is currently only supported by self-reported survey data.

insights.claim: Ben Carlson argues gambling must stay out of brokerage and retirement accounts, because a lack of friction lets people drain a brokerage account into sports-betting losses, and prediction markets wrapped inside ETFs are already coming with regulators showing no interest.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Flags an unpriced regulatory risk for brokerages and issuers commingling wagering products with retirement assets - a future headline risk if losses become visible.
insights.quote: There needs to be a little bit of friction to slow people down from making bad decisions.

insights.claim: The ETF proliferation cycle has barely begun - after prediction markets in ETFs, there will be an enormous volume of product thrown against the wall, in what amounts to a wild-west regulatory environment.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson and Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for ETF issuers and exchanges listing novelty products, and rising odds of an eventual investor-harm story that triggers regulation.

insights.claim: Parlay-style side bets have spread to casino table games: at a $15 blackjack table nearly every player was putting money on 9-to-1 and 100-to-1 three-card side bets, with the dealer steadily funneling money away from them.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Ground-level evidence that lottery-ticket payoff preference has spread beyond sportsbooks - the same demand curve that supports zero-day options and single-stock leveraged products.
insights.quote: It's crazy that these parlays are everywhere and people everyone is betting them almost every time.

insights.claim: Path dependency dominates investor satisfaction: a stock that goes 300 to 500 and back to 400 leaves the holder miserable despite the gain, while one that goes 300 to 200 back to 300 leaves them elated with no gain at all.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Explains why holders sell winners that round-trip and hold losers that recover - useful for anticipating flow behavior after sharp drawdowns and rebounds.
insights.quote: If you own a stock and it goes from 300 to 500 and then it falls back to 400, you've made a nice gain in that stock, but you're kind of miserable.

themes.theme: Gen Z balance sheets, renting, and the 401k verdict

insights.claim: Gen Z is measurably better off than prior generations at the same age on income, stock market dollars and wealth by age, with under-40s holding more money in the stock market than ever before - the opposite of the financial-nihilism narrative.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Supports a structurally larger, younger retail equity investor base than the doom narrative implies - relevant to brokerage account growth and long-run flows.
insights.quote: Gen Z really is better off in terms of income, in terms of stock market dollars, in terms of wealth by age.

insights.claim: The one legitimate young-person grievance is housing, not markets: missing 3% mortgage rates and lower prices by a few years is a genuine, not self-inflicted, setback.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Separates a real structural affordability problem from a manufactured sentiment story - housing, not equities, is where generational policy pressure will build.

insights.claim: Permanent renting by choice is set to become far more pervasive among young people, with money that would have been a down payment redirected into low-cost broad-based index funds instead.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: A structural flow argument: savings that historically went into home equity moving into equity funds instead, which would support brokerage AUM at housing's expense.
insights.quote: I love knowing that my rent is basically the maximum I'll pay in housing costs

insights.claim: The 401k has been a resounding success rather than a failed experiment: when it was created in the late 1970s only 38% of US private sector workers had pensions, and there was never a golden age of universal pension coverage.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Debunks the pension-nostalgia premise behind retirement-policy critiques; the counterfactual was no coverage, not lifetime pensions.

insights.claim: There is $10 trillion in 401k plans, 65% US stock market ownership would not exist without them, and Fidelity alone has 600,000 accounts worth $1 million or more - a number set to compound over the next decade or two.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson and Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Quantifies the automatic, price-insensitive bid under US equities from defined-contribution flows - the structural buyer most bear cases ignore.
insights.quote: Just at Fidelity alone, there are 600,000 accounts that are worth a million that have a million dollars or more.

insights.claim: About 40% of US workers still lack access to a 401k because their small-business employer does not offer one, and Ben Carlson's policy proposal is a Thrift Savings Plan-style government option open to anyone earning a paycheck.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: If universal-access retirement legislation ever advances, it would be a multi-trillion-dollar structural flow event for low-cost index providers and recordkeepers.

insights.claim: The 2008 crisis felt unifying because there were essentially no young rich people then, whereas today's visible cohort of wealthy young influencers creates a different, more resentful sentiment wavelength for those who feel left behind.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Explains why sentiment surveys can be terrible while aggregate balance sheets are strong - relative comparison, not absolute wealth, drives the readings.

insights.claim: Ben Carlson predicts the next recession's sentiment reaction function will be unusual because a meaningful share of the population - perhaps 20-30% - will quietly welcome a downturn as a leveling event.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Warns that consumer sentiment indices may behave unpredictably in the next downturn, weakening their usefulness as a real-time economic signal.
insights.quote: some people are going to be happy when we have the next recession

insights.claim: A structural side effect of so many newly rich parents is a coming cohort of downwardly mobile, unhappy heirs who will not match their parents' success - a small but growing segment.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Relevant to wealth-management demand: the great wealth transfer creates advisory and behavioral needs distinct from the wealth-accumulation client.

themes.theme: Cracks in rich-guy finance and private credit opacity

insights.claim: The allegations around the Dodgers and former Lakers owner, tied to his running of Guggenheim with private credit and insurance company dealings, illustrate that it is extremely easy to hide problems inside private equity and private credit - and this may be the next risk.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick and Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Names private credit opacity as the most plausible source of the next negative surprise, since even an NBA ownership vetting process failed to surface it.
insights.quote: it's really really easy to hide stuff if you need to

insights.claim: Matt Ishbia's mortgage company - one of the largest in the country - needed a rescue from Oaktree after putting on rate hedges that assumed rates would fall, and the stock is down 85% amid nonexistent housing activity.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson and Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: A live example of duration/rate-bet losses inside mortgage finance; watch originators whose business models were built on a rate-cut assumption that never arrived.
insights.quote: the stock's down 85%. I think they put some rate hedges on assuming rates would fall.

insights.claim: The composition of the top 1% and top 5% turns over far more often than people assume, and being very rich provides no guarantee of staying there even if money is easier to keep than in the past.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Argues against treating elite wealth as a permanent, stable capital pool - relevant when underwriting the durability of private-market limited-partner commitments.
insights.quote: the ranks of really rich people changes way more often than people think

insights.claim: Michael Batnick would impose a minimum five-year holding period on sports franchise ownership, warning that with valuations rising a billion dollars every two years, teams risk becoming pure financial assets flipped by owners with no regard for fan experience.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Sports teams are being institutionalized as an asset class; a $2.5 billion gain in 18 months is exactly the return profile that attracts financial buyers and eventual league-level restrictions.
insights.quote: if it is purely purely a financial asset and there's little consideration to the experience of the fans, what is that going to do to the league?

insights.claim: SpaceX bounced from 100 to roughly 150 during its share unlock after everyone had focused on whether it would break below 100 - a clean example of negativity bias, and Ben Carlson took a quick 20% gain on it.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick and Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Pre-IPO/secondary unlock fears were mispriced here; unlock-driven selloffs in hot private names have been fade-able rather than trend-setting.
insights.quote: Is anybody talking about the fact that it just bounced from 100 to buck 50 during the unlock?

insights.claim: The share of Americans who flew in the past 12 months has roughly doubled from about 25% in the 1970s to nearly 50%, and the inflation-adjusted cost of a domestic flight has been cut in half since the early 1990s.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson, citing Bloomberg
insights.so_what: Real airfare deflation with volume doubling is the clearest illustration in the episode of why airlines are a terrible business despite booming demand.
insights.quote: the cost of a domestic flight has essentially been cut in half
